Q195.L1t: Peak expiratory flow meters are simple handheld devices used to measure how fast a person can exhale air from the lungs.
Q195.L2t: Serial peak flow readings are typically taken morning and evening, often over about two weeks, to look for how much the measurements vary.
Q195.L3t: Diagnostic value comes from marked diurnal or day-to-day variability in airflow, which reflects reversible airway narrowing, a hallmark of one particular obstructive condition and not of fixed obstruction or infections.
Q195.L4t: Peak flow variation over two weeks is diagnostic in asthma.
Q195.L2f: Peak flow readings are always taken only once, in a clinic, and are never recorded at home over several days.
Q195.L3f: Fixed, progressive airflow obstruction in chronic smokers produces large day-to-day swings in peak flow, which is the defining feature used to diagnose that chronic lung disease.
Q195.L4f: Serial peak flow variation over two weeks is diagnostic in COPD.

Q196.L1t: Proteins are large biological macromolecules built from smaller units called amino acids and have many roles in living cells.
Q196.L2t: Amino acids join in a condensation reaction that releases a molecule of water as each new link in the chain forms.
Q196.L3t: The covalent link between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next is a carbon–nitrogen amide linkage that forms the backbone of the polypeptide chain.
Q196.L4t: Amino acids in a protein are linked by peptide bonds.
Q196.L2f: Amino acids are joined in a hydrolysis reaction that consumes water, and the polypeptide chain is made of identical repeating units.
Q196.L3f: The backbone of a protein is built from bonds formed by full electron transfer between oppositely charged amino acid side groups, creating charged attraction that holds the chain together.
Q196.L4f: Amino acids in a protein are linked by ionic bonds.

Q197.L1t: Dopamine is a catecholamine drug given by intravenous infusion, with dose rates commonly expressed per kilogram of body weight per minute.
Q197.L2t: Infusion calculations require converting between micrograms and milligrams, where 1 milligram equals 1000 micrograms, and between minutes and hours.
Q197.L3t: Multiply 4 micrograms by 65 kg to get the dose per minute, then multiply by 60 minutes, and divide the resulting micrograms by 1000 to convert to milligrams.
Q197.L4t: The person will receive 15.6 milligrams in an hour.
Q197.L2f: Dopamine infusion rates are always calculated in milligrams per kilogram per hour, so no unit conversion between micrograms and milligrams is ever needed.
Q197.L3f: To convert micrograms to milligrams you divide by 100, and the per-minute dose of 260 micrograms is then multiplied by 60 minutes.
Q197.L4f: The person will receive 156 milligrams in an hour.
